**Personhood** — what a person is and what makes one persist — personal identity over time, psychological continuity and what matters in survival, persons as bearers of reasons, rights and responsibility. Not the self, which is self (group: philosophy; ADR-024).

| [THEORY-060](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-060.md) v2 | Life story is the form of diachronic identity | McAdams (2019), [LIT-595](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-595.md): narrative identity is "a person's internalized and evolving story of how he or she has become the person he or she is becoming", which gives a life "unity, moral purpose, and temporal coherence". It arrives in adolescence and young adulthood, on the back of autobiographical memory and autobiographical reasoning, as the third layer of a psychological self after the actor of traits and the agent of goals. Stories with agentic and redemptive themes go with well-being and generativity, and in one longitudinal therapy study the story "changes first, and then the storyteller gets better". A review essay: every finding is cited, not shown, and it concedes that having a life story may be a modern cultural construction. Strawson's "Against Narrativity" ([LIT-452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-452.md)) denies the first half for many people. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-065](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-065.md) | Collective agents are agents in the same sense | Korsgaard (2014), [LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md): an action is a movement "backed by the agent as a whole", and ordinary attribution implies that the agent was active and that the action expresses who she is. Following the categorical and hypothetical imperatives gives action the form of self-determined efficacy; the content of the maxims chosen under that form constitutes practical identity. Self-consciousness of one's own attitudes breaks the unity an animal is given, and reason is the work of rebuilding it, so unity of agency "is an achievement, not a given", and people can act together "in the most literal sense". The Tanner Lectures ([LIT-564](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-564.md)) supply the reflective structure the chapter assumes. Argued, with the Kantian premise assumed and the collective mechanism stated in a paragraph. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-075](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-075.md) | Moral obligation follows from valuing humanity | Korsgaard (1992), [LIT-564](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-564.md): because human consciousness is reflective, an agent must act on reasons, and so must identify with some law, a "practical identity": "a description under which you value yourself". "Your reasons express your identity, your nature; your obligations spring from what that identity forbids." Obligation is "the reflective rejection of a threat to your identity", unconditional where violation would be worse than death. Identities are a "jumble" and differ across social worlds, so this much yields no morality. Moral obligation enters because valuing any identity requires valuing one's humanity, the source of all one's reasons. "The Normative Constitution of Agency" ([LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md)) later makes practical identity the content of maxims chosen under the formal norms. Argued, with the key steps flagged by their author as sketchy; the commentaries and reply are unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-076](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-076.md) | Self-governance is intrapersonal shared intention | Bratman (2018), [LIT-567](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-567.md): an agent governs herself over time when she is self-governing at each time along a planned activity and her intentions at those times interlock as the intentions of people acting together do, so that she acts "together" with herself. Her standpoints include a conditional, reflexive end of her own diachronic self-governance, which is what lets resolve against temptation be self-governed while following through on Kavka's toxin is not. He rejects the bargaining model (McClennen, Ainslie) in two sentences and calls narrative unity less basic in one. A philosophical model argued from cases; the analogy is partial by its author's account and its terms come from a book the record has not read. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-120](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-120.md) v2 | Free will is identification with one's motives | Frankfurt's hierarchical, or endorsement, account, from his own texts: the 1971 paper ([LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md), read) and the 2004 Tanner Lectures ([LIT-293](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-293.md), read). A person's will is the desire that moves him to act; he identifies with a desire by wanting it to be his will, decisively, and he acts of his own free will when the will that moves him is the will he wants. In 2004 the condition is "volitional unanimity" with no conflict "at any higher order", and identification is "willing acceptance", which may be resigned. Acting of one's own free will is what responsibility requires, and alternatives and history are irrelevant. The 1987 and 1992 revisions are held only by report. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-131](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-131.md) v2 | CID structures make corporations agents | French (1979), [LIT-727](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-727.md). Moral persons are non-eliminable subjects of accountability, so intentional agents. A corporation's CID Structure licenses redescribing members' acts as corporate acts, and an act that implements established corporate policy is done for corporate reasons. Proposed: the step from agency to moral personhood is asserted, and corporate intentionality is shown by licensed redescription, not by any test. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-417](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-417.md) v2 | Personal identity is several separate questions | Olson (2002; rev. 2023), [LIT-454](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-454.md), read in [NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md). | [THEORY-447](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-447.md) v2 | What matters in survival is not identity | Parfit (1971), [LIT-447](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-447.md), read in [NOTE-378](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-378.md), with the fission dilemma as Olson's survey states it, [LIT-454](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-454.md) ([NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md)). | [THEORY-464](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-464.md) v2 | Ethics turns on relations other than identity | Dufner (2025), [LIT-130](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-130.md), the SEP entry that replaced Shoemaker's, read in [NOTE-166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-166.md). | [THEORY-476](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-476.md) | Stage-aggregate persons make identity matter | Lewis (1976), [LIT-446](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-446.md), read in [NOTE-373](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-373.md). Shown: that identity being one-one and all-or-nothing, and what matters branching and coming in degrees, do not entail that identity is not what matters, once stages and continuants are told apart; and that under supervaluation degrees of I-relatedness equal degrees of R-relatedness. Stipulated: that persons are the maximal R-interrelated aggregates. Conceded as costly: counting persons by tensed identity, which "is not a kind of identity". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-531](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-531.md) v2 | First vs third person: opposite identity verdicts | Williams (1970), [LIT-462](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-462.md), read in [NOTE-387](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-387.md). The strongest step is shown given its premise: the last step of the series that turns amnesia into a body exchange changes nothing for the subject. The premise, that psychological change cannot remove the reason to fear pain, is argued from cases. Williams claims no criterion of identity, calls his resolution "rather shaky" and "risky", and does not treat fission. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-546](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-546.md) v2 | Persons persist by psychological continuity | Locke (1694), [LIT-464](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-464.md), read in [NOTE-385](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-385.md), with the repairs as Olson's survey ([LIT-454](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-454.md), [NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md)) and Parfit ([LIT-447](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-447.md), [NOTE-378](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-378.md)) give them. Locke shows that same man, same substance and same person can be given different conditions; that the person's are those of consciousness he asserts and illustrates. The repaired criterion is the majority view in the survey, and its author, an animalist, argues it implies two thinkers in every chair. It is a criterion of persistence, not an account of what matters or of what we are made of. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-590](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-590.md) | Autonomy's self is not identity's self | Velleman (2002), [LIT-292](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-292.md), read in [NOTE-268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-268.md). A critique of Frankfurt's late (1990s) view that autonomy is governance by the essential character of the will, an essence that is also the condition of one's identity. It argues by counterexample (Winnicott's False Self, the Agamemnon sequel), from Freud's Rat Man, and by debunking genealogy. The positive view, that "self" marks reflexivity and that autonomous action is motivated in part by the understanding, is stated "briefly" and argued elsewhere. Frankfurt's reply is unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-650](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-650.md) | Diachronic self-identity is level-relative | Floridi (2011), [LIT-136](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-136.md), read in [NOTE-130](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-130.md). The deflation of diachronic identity is an informal argument from examples that rests on the method of levels of abstraction, assumed from elsewhere; that this "is not relativism" is one sentence, and that individuation comes before identification is asserted. It is not, as its title suggests, a criterion of personal identity, and its positive answer to the synchronic question, the three-membranes model, is "somewhat figurative" by its author's word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-681](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-681.md) | The self is a bundle of perceptions | Hume (1739, with the Appendix of 1740), [LIT-451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-451.md), read in [NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md). | [THEORY-1572](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1572.md) v2 | We are essentially embodied wills | Johnston (2023), [LIT-1788](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1788.md), read in [NOTE-1257](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1257.md) in place of Surviving Death ([LIT-1759](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1759.md)). | [THEORY-1609](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1609.md) v2 | Low future-self similarity predicts impatience | Hershfield (2011), [LIT-1702](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1702.md), read in [NOTE-1259](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1259.md) from the accepted manuscript. | [THEORY-1610](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1610.md) v2 | Wide person-affecting view solves non-identity | Parfit's last paper (2017), read in full and unfinished by the editor's note ([NOTE-1263](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1263.md)). | [THEORY-1671](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1671.md) | Child genital surgery only if strictly necessary | The Brussels Collaboration on Bodily Integrity, read in [NOTE-1799](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1799.md) (Skimmed). Restricting itself to nonvoluntary genital cutting or surgery by licensed clinicians on prepubescent children in Global North healthcare systems, and taking no position on criminal law or religious practice outside healthcare, the collaboration argues: there is a near-universal consensus that clinicians may not perform any medically unnecessary genital procedure on endosex girls, however minimal; the sound reasons for that consensus are not benefit–risk calculations but respect for privacy, bodily integrity, developing sexual boundaries and future genital autonomy; those reasons apply equally to intersex children and endosex boys; so clinicians should perform no nonvoluntary genital cutting or surgery on any child unless it is medically necessary in a strict sense (a serious, time-sensitive threat to physical health, no less invasive or postponable alternative, preserving future choice).
